newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end mixed, long, short ends diverge.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end mixed, long, short ends diverge.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended a quiet session broadly mixed on Friday, with the lion's share of the losses concentrated in long end of the yield curve.
The 30-year bond fell 17/32 to 100-1/2, while its yield edged up to 6.46 percent from 6.42 on Thursday. The two-year note was off 1/32 at 100-12/32, yielding 5.67 percent.
"There are two distinct classes of trade," said Michael McClure, head trader at Zions First National Bank, explaining that the long and short ends are trading independently of each other.
McClure said he saw "significant" buying at the short end from retail accounts, mainly in one- to three-year maturities.
"That part of the market is cheap," he said. "The long bond is in its own world."
Traders said profit-taking weighed on the long bond in this session.

Meanwhile, bill rates rose on Friday, led by a two-basis-point rise in the three-month bill to 5.01 percent. Six-month bills edged up to 5.05 percent, while the year bill was unchanged at 5.11 percent, although the year bill had been lower much of the session.
Despite sluggishness at the long end, market participants didn't appear to be concerned.
"It was just profit-taking before the weekend," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "There's still a very bullish tone to the market.
"There is a nervousness in that the market has moved so quickly and so much over a short period. How much further can it go without concrete evidence the economy is slowing further?" she added.

News that the manufacturing sector slowed in October had little impact on prices, since the 0.5-percent drop in industrial production was skewed by a strike at General Motors Corp that has since ended.
Still, factory output fell 0.1 percent excluding autos, suggesting a weak start to the fourth quarter for the economy.

But the market caught the jitters at mid-morning, after the University of Michigan reported that its consumer sentiment index rose to 98.9 in November from 96.5 in October. The current conditions and expectations indexes also jumped.
Also, U.S. business inventories rose 0.1 percent in September.
Market participants said that with no key economic news until the November employment report due in a few weeks, the market should do better in the near term.
The focus now shifts to supply, as the Treasury sells $18.25 billion two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
Analysts predict the auctions will go well, given the slim-to-nil chance for a rate hike anytime soon.
Scott Pardee, senior advisor at Yamaichi International (America) Inc, said talk has increased that the Fed's next move will be an ease, but added, "That's a ways off."
He said prospects look bright for the market going forward, even though a softer dollar has decreased the number of foreign buyers over the past few days.

"I expect the long bond to go down to 6.25 percent by year end," he said. "We still will have sluggish numbers coming out ... Europe has rallied, but there are still a lot of questions about the EMU. So, the U.S. looks good compared to other countries." -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
